summary.text: Paramecium is a genus of single-celled ciliates, widespread in freshwater, brackish and ocean environments.
It propels itself by whip-like movements of cilia arranged in tightly spaced rows around its body, spiralling through the water.
Some species are easy to grow and induce to conjugate and divide, so Paramecium is widely used in classrooms and labs to study biological processes.

facts.label: Body covering
facts.value: A stiff but elastic structure called the pellicle

facts.label: Vacuole acidity
facts.value: Contents drop from pH 7 to 3 within five minutes

facts.label: Trichocysts
facts.value: Explosive organelles that discharge thin, non-toxic filaments

facts.label: Energy spent swimming
facts.value: More than half of its energy

items.prompt: A swimming Paramecium bumps into a pebble. What does it do?

options.label: Keeps pressing forward until the pebble gives way
Swims backward briefly, then tries again
Stops moving until the pebble drifts off
Curls its body around the pebble

items.explain: Its cilia reverse their effective stroke so it swims backward briefly, and it repeats this until it can get past the object.

items.prompt: How does a Paramecium bring food into its cell?

options.label: Cilia lining an oral groove beat continuously and draw food in
Contractile vacuoles suck food in
Trichocysts harpoon prey and pull it inward
The pellicle pulses and squeezes food through

items.explain: A deep oral groove is lined with cilia that beat continuously, drawing food into the cell.

items.prompt: Cilia propulsion in Paramecium is under 1 percent efficient. How should that be read?

options.label: It shows cilia are a poor design that is likely to be replaced
It means Paramecium mostly drifts instead of swimming
It happens because its cilia beat out of step
It is close to the maximum possible for cilia as short as theirs

items.explain: This low percentage is nevertheless close to the maximum theoretical efficiency for an organism with cilia as short as Paramecium's.

items.prompt: Pond water keeps seeping into a Paramecium by osmosis. What deals with it?

options.label: Contractile vacuoles that actively expel the water
The anal pore, which releases it with waste
The trichocysts, which soak it up
Food vacuoles, which digest it

items.explain: Osmoregulation is carried out by contractile vacuoles, which actively expel water to compensate for fluid absorbed by osmosis.

items.prompt: A food vacuole starts circulating through a Paramecium. What happens inside it as digestion goes on?

options.label: Its contents turn steadily more alkaline
Enzymes enter and its contents turn more acidic
Cilia inside it grind the food down
It passes out undigested through the cell mouth

items.explain: Enzymes from the cytoplasm enter the vacuole to digest the contents, and as digestion proceeds the contents become more acidic.

items.prompt: Most Paramecium eat bacteria and other small organisms, yet a few species also get nutrients another way. How?

options.label: From chloroplasts grown in their cilia
By absorbing minerals through the pellicle
From endosymbiotic algae carried in their cytoplasm
By digesting their own trichocysts

items.explain: A few species are mixotrophs, deriving some nutrients from endosymbiotic algae (chlorella) carried in the cytoplasm.

paragraphs.heading: A single-celled pond dweller
paragraphs.text: Paramecium is a genus of single-celled ciliates found in fresh water, brackish water and the sea. They are often plentiful in still ponds and pools. A cell is 0.06 to 0.3 mm long and usually oval, elongated, or shaped like a foot or a cigar.

paragraphs.heading: Lab rats of the ciliates
paragraphs.text: Some species are easy to grow and to prompt into conjugating and dividing, so they are widely used in classrooms and labs. They have been called the lab rats of the ciliate phylum. Microscopists first saw them in the late 17th century, and Christiaan Huygens described them clearly in a letter in 1678. Through the 18th and 19th centuries they were nicknamed the slipper animalcule, and the name Paramecium, from a Greek word for oblong, was coined by John Hill in 1752.

paragraphs.heading: The cell's outer layer
paragraphs.text: The cell is wrapped in a pellicle, a covering that is stiff but elastic. It has three layers: the outer cell membrane, a layer of flat sacs known as alveoli, and an inner layer, the epiplasm. Its surface is dimpled with six-sided or rectangular hollows, and a single cilium pokes out through a hole in the middle of each. Between the sacs most species have trichocysts, organelles that fire thin non-toxic threads, often for defence.

paragraphs.heading: How it swims
paragraphs.text: A paramecium moves by beating its cilia, which grow in tightly packed rows around the body. Each beat has a quick, stiff effective stroke and then a slow recovery stroke, in which the cilium curls to one side and sweeps forward. Waves of beating pass across the cilia, a bit like wind over a field of grain, and the cell spirals as it goes. If it bumps into something, it reverses its effective stroke, backs up briefly, and tries again until it gets past. This is called the avoidance reaction.

paragraphs.heading: Costly swimming
paragraphs.text: Getting around is expensive for a paramecium. By one calculation it spends more than half its energy on moving, and its way of swimming is less than 1% efficient. Even so, that is close to the best that cilia as short as these could manage in theory.

paragraphs.heading: Eating and digesting
paragraphs.text: Paramecium mostly eats small organisms such as bacteria, algae and yeasts. Its cilia sweep prey and some water down the oral groove, a channel lined with cilia that beat all the time. From there food moves into the gullet and through the cytostome, or cell mouth. Inside, the food is gathered into food vacuoles that break off and travel around the cell on its streaming contents. Enzymes enter each vacuole and digest the food, and within five minutes the pH inside drops from 7 to 3.

paragraphs.heading: Water and partners
paragraphs.text: Water keeps seeping into the cell by osmosis, and contractile vacuoles actively push it back out. How many of these vacuoles a cell has depends on the species. A few species carry algae called chlorella inside them and get some of their nutrients from these partners.
